messages.author: 9b8fc0ee8fc61aa5
messages.subject: Using the WITH_LIBTMB in an R package
parts:
Firstly, thanks a lot for great package. I have saved a tremendous amount of time on my postdoc because of the package.

Description

I have extensively used the TMB package to implement variational approximations for mixed survival models and joint marker and survival models. The package can be found here: github.com/boennecd/survTMB

Because the project has grown quite a bit, I really needed: 

  1. Multiple .cpp files to reduce the compilation time when developing.
  2. Make my own interface to CppAD with the additional features from TMB (see MGMS.cpp, heritability.cpp, and joint.cpp). Doing this with Rcpp is convenient.
  3. Have my own CppAD::atomic_base implementations of particular Gauss-Legendre quadrature and Gauss-Hermite quadrature to reduce the memory usage and computation substantially (see snva-utils.h#L71-L503, gva-utils.h#L29-L231, and joint-utils.h). 
  4. Have a number other C++ functions which I needed and get access to them with Rcpp. 
  5. Have unit test in C++ with Catch through the testthat package (see the "test-..." files in /src directory).
The way I have done this it by having a single .cpp which includes TMB.hpp (tmb.cpp) while all other files includes a header which defines WITH_LIBTMB (tmb_includes.h) and some macros so I can use TMB with Rcpp.

Questions
  1. Is this recommend / will this be supported? 
  2. Further, is there a way to reduce the size of the .dll/.so file afterwards? The final packages takes 130 MB on Ubuntu with gcc-8 (though with -g). It might though be because of RcppArmadillo and RcppEigen packages too.
Another question which might be for a separate post but I will include it here. I implemented the following function here: utils.h#L64-L73

to conditional skip region which anyway are not computed by this thread like e.g. here: snva.cpp#L79-L83

This is useful as it reduces the memory requirement both when evaluating the parallel tapes but also the final memory requirement (which I have seen some post about). It also reduced the computation time in my example. I gather something similar is useful in numerous other applications. 

The issue is that I heavily rely on the current parallel_region implementation (tmb_core.hpp#L693-L700). Thus, is this going to be stable or? 

Suggestion
Regarding the later, then maybe one can make a operator() function where the user passes in the lambda functions like below? This might not be too hard to explain and then the instruction would be e.g. in a grouped data settings to tell the user to pass the complete data log-likelihood factor for each group in a separate lambda function? 

class parallel_add {
    double val = 0.;
    int counter = 0L;
    
public:    
    template<class F>
    void operator()(F f) {
        if(counter++ % 2 == 0)
            /* no work */
            return;
        
        double const new_val = f();
        std::cout << "Added " << new_val << '\n';
        val += new_val;
    }
    
    operator double() const {
        return val;
    }
};

int main(){
    parallel_add adder;
    adder([&](){ return 1.; });
    adder([&](){ return 2.; });
    adder([&](){ return 3.; });
    adder([&](){ return 4.; });
    
    std::cout << "Final value is " << (double)adder << '\n';
    return 0;
}


See http://cpp.sh/9vztz.

messages.author: 258b98968d0ad8b9
messages.subject: Re: Using the WITH_LIBTMB in an R package
parts:
1. Yes! The way you set up 'tmb_includes.h' and 'tmb.cpp' is the intentional way (setting WITH_LIBTMB to get declarations and TMB_PRECOMPILE to get definitions). It bothers me a bit that you have to redefine a bunch of macros to avoid conflicts with Rcpp. Somtime in the future this should be fixed in TMB but it will have to wait for now.

I have one comment though. Your setup is tied to CppAD and won't be able to take advantage of the future AD library (branch TMBad) which at some point may become the default. This is not a problem: There will be a flag to explicitly select CppAD.

2. I'm not aware of any simple way to reduce the *.so size except by setting the compiler flag as in https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/wiki/FAQ (bottom) which won't be allowed by CRAN. Ideally one would like to eliminate symbol duplicates so that symbols in tmb.o are not present elsewhere, e.g. compare:

nm tmb.o | grep CppAD6ADTapeIdE13RecordCondExp

with

nm *.o | grep CppAD6ADTapeIdE13RecordCondExp

Then compare with with a symbol you actually precompiled.
It would be nice if, sometime in the future, a larger portion of TMB could be precompiled (without performance side effects).

To you suggestion: I think this idea is essentially the same as the (undocumented) macro 'PARALLEL_REGION' defined here

https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/07678703541b81966f18f134d7d7cbf5df9e3345/TMB/inst/include/tmb_core.hpp#L346

and used in

https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/master/tmb_examples/register_atomic_parallel.cpp

to avoid taping unnecessary operations?

The idea of using lambda functions looks interesting. So far I deliberately avoided relying on C++11 features because until recently C++98 was the default in R.

This is useful as it reduces the memory requirement both when evaluating the parallel tapes but also the final memory requirement (which I have seen some post about). It also reduced the computation time in my example. I gather something similar is useful in numerous other applications.

Suggestion
Regarding the later, then maybe one can make a operator() function where the user passes in the lambda functions like below? This might not be too hard to explain and then the instruction would be e.g. in a grouped data settings to tell the user to pass the complete data log-likelihood factor for each group in a separate lambda function? 

class parallel_add {
    double val = 0.;
    int counter = 0L;
    
public:    
    template<class F>
    void operator()(F f) {
        if(counter++ % 2 == 0)
            /* no work */
            return;
        
        double const new_val = f();
        std::cout << "Added " << new_val << '\n';
        val += new_val;
    }
    
    operator double() const {
        return val;
    }
};

int main(){
    parallel_add adder;
    adder([&](){ return 1.; });
    adder([&](){ return 2.; });
    adder([&](){ return 3.; });
    adder([&](){ return 4.; });
    
    std::cout << "Final value is " << (double)adder << '\n';
    return 0;
}
